item.mechanism: Rapid solidification inherent to the LPBF process results in a finer grain size compared to conventional arc melting, which contributes to higher compressive strength.
item.system: HEA WTaMoNbV produced by Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using mixed elemental powder
item.operating_conditions: LPBF process with advanced trials parameters (244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density)
item.supporting_observation: The LPBF sample exhibited a finer grain size (average 10 µm) compared to the AMF sample (average 25 µm) and a higher ultimate compressive strength (1391 MPa vs 1107 MPa).
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is inferred from the comparison of grain sizes and strength; the text notes that further optimization and post-heat treatments are needed to fully rectify defects.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that differences in powder particle shape and size (irregular vs spherical) could also influence the solidification process and elemental distribution.
quotes: The relatively increased compressive strength of the LPBF sample could be related to the relatively reduced grain size, due to inherent rapid solidification characteristics.
In general, this reveals the presence of a single solid phase solution with a relatively fine grain size (average size 10 µm).
Although the counterpart alloy also presents a single solid phase solution structure, its grain size was significantly increased compared to the LPBF samples (average size 25 µm).

item.mechanism: The large difference in melting temperatures between Tungsten (3422 °C) and Vanadium (1910 °C) causes Vanadium to solidify last, leading to its segregation at grain boundaries.
item.system: HEA WTaMoNbV produced by both LPBF and Arc Melting Furnace (AMF)
item.operating_conditions: Solidification during LPBF and AMF processing
item.supporting_observation: EDS analysis showed significant depletion of W and substantial increase in V at grain boundaries in AMF samples, and high W in bright grains in LPBF samples, attributed to melting point differences.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains elemental distribution but does not account for all microstructural differences; the text notes that powder shape deviations also influence the process.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the irregular shape and size of the mixed elemental powders could affect laser beam operation and solidification differently than spherical pre-alloyed powders.
quotes: This phenomenon can be attributed to the relatively low melting temperature of V, which consequently solidified at the end of the solidification process, and hence was found to prefer grain boundaries.
This can be attributed mainly to the relatively high melting temperature and high density of W compared to other alloying elements.

This can mainly be related to the relatively low melting temperature of vanadium (1910 °C) versus tungsten (3422 °C), which consequently causes vanadium to solidify at grain boundaries during the final phase of the solidification process.

item.mechanism: Insufficient local energy density during the LPBF process leads to inadequate fusion of consecutive powder layers, resulting in lack-of-fusion defects and porosity.
item.system: HEA WTaMoNbV produced by LPBF during primary and intermediate trials
item.operating_conditions: LPBF trials with lower energy densities (38.1 J/mm³ to 109.1 J/mm³)
item.supporting_observation: Primary trials showed 38% density and significant lack-of-fusion defects, while advanced trials with higher energy density (162.7 J/mm³) achieved 95% density and fewer defects.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically to the early trials with low energy density; advanced trials with optimized parameters minimized these defects.
item.alternatives_considered: The text mentions that differences in powder particle shape and size could also affect flowability and fusion, but explicitly links the defects in primary trials to energy density.
quotes: Apparently, the relatively large amount of binding defects found in the primary LPBF trials can be related to inadequate fusion of consecutive powder layers.
This can be attributed to the insufficient local energy density that is required for proper layer fusion.
The differences between the primary, on the one hand, and the intermediate and advanced LPBF trials, on the other, in terms of densities, were 38% and 95%, respectively.

item.mechanism: Residual stresses generated during the additive manufacturing process cause shifts in XRD diffraction peaks compared to conventionally produced alloys.
item.operating_conditions: Post-LPBF state, analyzed via X-ray diffraction
item.supporting_observation: Small peak shifts were observed in the LPBF samples in comparison to the AMF sample in the XRD analysis.
item.scope_limits: The text states these are 'normal residual stresses' and does not quantify the stress magnitude or its effect on long-term stability.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that differences in peak intensities could be related to preferred orientation, but noted that XRD results showed no significant sign of preferred orientation between printing directions.
quotes: In addition, small peak shifts were observed in the LPBF samples in comparison to the AMF sample.
The shifting of these peaks can be related to normal residual stresses that are produced during the additive manufacturing process.

item.mechanism: High-density dislocations and sub-grains form within the alloy matrix due to internal stresses inherently generated by the rapid thermal cycling of the LPBF process.
item.operating_conditions: LPBF processed material, analyzed via Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)
item.supporting_observation: TEM analysis demonstrated the presence of sub-grains (approx. 500 nm) and high-density dislocations in the alloy matrix.
item.scope_limits: The text does not quantify the dislocation density or its specific contribution to mechanical properties beyond the general inference of brittleness.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors noted that precipitates were also observed but did not decode their structure due to difficulty in finding different ordinations.
quotes: This high-resolution observation demonstrates the presence of sub-grains, with a size of about 500 nm, that compose the alloy matrix.
Furthermore, evidence of high-density dislocations was also observed, and is probably due to common internal stresses inherently generated by the LPBF process.
In addition, relatively small precipitates with a size of 60–80 nm and with a nearly spherical shape were dispersed along the intergranular boundaries.

item.mechanism: The relatively increased surface roughness of the LPBF alloy reduces passivation stability, manifested by current density fluctuations, despite having a higher break potential.
item.operating_conditions: Electrochemical testing in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature
item.supporting_observation: Potentiodynamic polarization showed current density fluctuations for the LPBF alloy, while the AMF alloy had easier passivation but lower stability and lower break potential.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is specific to the corrosion behavior in 3.5% NaCl; the text notes that localized corrosion attack (pit dimensions) was actually reduced in the LPBF alloy despite the roughness.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the non-homogeneous characteristics of the LPBF sample and inherent printing defects contribute to the differences in corrosion mechanism.
quotes: In addition, due to the relatively increased roughness of the LPBF alloy, its passivation stability manifested by current density fluctuations was reduced.
This basically means that although the passivation of the AMF alloy is easier to obtain, its stability is reduced.

item.mechanism: The presence of porosity and unmelted powder particles on the fracture surface induces brittleness in the LPBF alloy.
item.operating_conditions: Compressive testing leading to fracture failure
item.supporting_observation: SEM fracture analysis revealed typical LPBF defects such as porosity and un-melted powder particles on the fracture surface, correlating with the brittle transgranular fracture morphology.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains the brittleness but the text also attributes the higher strength to the finer grain size, suggesting a complex interplay of factors.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that differences in microstructure and solidification defects generally contribute to the mechanical behavior, not just the specific defects.
quotes: In addition, Figure 9 c,d indicates that the fracture surface contains typical LPBF defects, such as porosity and un-melted powder particles that induce brittleness.
The fracture failure analysis of the LPBF and AMF samples obtained by SEM revealed a relatively brittle fracture with a transgranular morphology.
The higher compressive strength and more brittle fracture of the LPBF alloy may be related to differences in the microstructure and solidification defects and in the finer grain size.

item.mechanism: The use of mixed elemental powders with irregular shapes and size deviations (e.g., Ta) leads to uneven distribution of elements compared to spherical pre-alloyed powders.
item.system: HEA WTaMoNbV produced by LPBF using mixed elemental powder
item.operating_conditions: LPBF process using mixed elemental powders with 20-70 µm size distribution
item.supporting_observation: The text notes a standard deviation of 20% for Ta size and links this to uneven distribution, contrasting with the expectation that spherical powders improve flowability and homogeneity.
item.scope_limits: This is a proposed mechanism for elemental distribution issues; the study found the overall composition was still relatively similar (deviations < 3.9%at) despite these local variations.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the high melting temperature of Ta combined with shape deviation leads to uneven distribution, but also noted that the overall chemical composition was similar to the AMF counterpart.
quotes: Additional reasons for the elemental distribution in the case of the LPBF process may be related to differences in the shape and size of the powder particles.
Their irregular size can affect the laser beam operation differently, and consequently influence the solidification process.

This may relate, for example, to the relatively Ta size deviation (standard deviation of 20%). The combination of the high melting temperature (3017 °C) of Ta and the relatively large shape deviation can lead to uneven distribution.
